entries.narration: This is where we are going. By the end of this course, Ana's own server, web-01, serves her website, ana dot example, over HTTPS. On the right, her laptop asks for the site: two hundred OK over HTTPS, a redirect from plain HTTP, and a certificate chain the laptop trusts. One honest note: that certificate comes from a small local certificate authority standing in for Let's Encrypt, because ana dot example is a name reserved for documentation, and can never be on the public internet. Everything else is exactly what you would run for real. The map on the left is the whole server, and every part on it is a lesson. A firewall that lets in only SSH and the web. Services run by systemd: SSH that accepts keys and nothing else, nginx serving the site, a journal of everything, and timers for security updates, a nightly report and log rotation. Two users, each with exactly the rights they need. And underneath, the Linux kernel on a small virtual machine. We will build all of it from an empty server, one command at a time, in the order a real server needs it: log in and look around, users and permissions, software, services, the website itself, logs and automation, and finally, keeping it running. Every command you see is real, typed into a real Debian server, with its real output. Where something is a stand in, it says so on screen. Let's start with what we are logging into.

Before we log in, a word on what we are logging into. Strictly speaking, Linux is only the kernel: the core program that manages processes, memory, files and the network. A distribution wraps that kernel with everything else you need, a package manager, default settings, and thousands of tools. Most distributions belong to one of two big families. The Debian family includes Debian itself and Ubuntu, which is built from it, and they install software with apt. The Red Hat family starts with Fedora, flows into Red Hat Enterprise Linux, and from there into free rebuilds such as Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, which install software with dnf. Others, like Arch and SUSE, have their own tools. This course runs on two real servers, one from each family. Web-01 runs Debian 13, and it is the server we will build. Web-02 runs Rocky Linux 10, and it appears whenever the two families do something differently. The terminals at the bottom ask each server the same two questions. uname reports the kernel: both are Linux six point twelve, built by each distribution. The os-release file names the distribution, and Rocky's even admits its ancestry with ID like: rhel, centos, fedora. And macOS? It is Unix-like, and its terminal will feel familiar, but it is not Linux, and a real Mac says so. Asked the same questions, uname answers Darwin, Apple's own kernel; there is no slash proc, and no os-release file at all. Its everyday tools are the BSD versions rather than GNU's, so a few options differ. Now, the first login.

Ana has rented a fresh server. The provider gave her an address and a password, and she connects from her laptop with ssh, the secure shell. ssh talks to a program on the server called sshd, the SSH server, which listens on port twenty two. Everything between them is encrypted. The first thing ssh says is a warning, and it is worth reading. The laptop has never met this server, so it cannot know whether it is talking to the real web-01 or to an impostor in between. It shows the server's key fingerprint, a short summary of the server's own identity key. A careful admin compares it with the one the provider publishes. Ana answers yes, and the laptop remembers this key in a file called known hosts. From now on, the check happens silently on every connection, and a different key would stop her with a loud warning. Then the password. Nothing appears as she types it, by design. After the server's welcome text comes the most important line on screen, the prompt. It says who you are, ana, which machine you are on, web-01, and where you are: the tilde means your home directory. The dollar sign says you are an ordinary user. whoami and hostname confirm the first two. Next, what you can type at that prompt.

Every command line has the same shape: words separated by spaces. The first word is the command, the program to run. The words after it are options, which change how the command behaves, and arguments, which say what it should work on. ls lists a directory, and in Ana's brand new home directory it prints nothing at all. That is normal: Unix tools stay silent when there is nothing to say. With dash l, a short option, ls prints the long format: one line per file, with permissions, owner, size and date. Here it lists the SSH server's own directory, including the host keys we just met. A short option is one dash and one letter. A long option is two dashes and a word, like human readable, which turns sizes into kilobytes and megabytes. Long options are easier to read in a script; short ones are quicker to type. Slash var slash log is the argument. How do you learn the options? Every command comes with a manual page, and man ls opens it in a pager, shown on the right. The top line says LS, one: section one of the manual, user commands. The manual has numbered sections, and the ones a server admin meets most are one for commands, five for configuration file formats, and eight for administration commands. Press q to leave the manual. Next, a tour of the whole file system.

On Linux, there are no drive letters. Everything lives in one tree, starting at the root, written as a single slash. ls slash lists its top level, and each directory there has a job. Slash etc holds configuration: plain text files that root edits, like the SSH settings and the hostname. Slash var holds data that changes while the server runs: logs live in slash var slash log, and later in this course Ana's website will live in slash var slash www. Slash home holds one directory per person; on this server, only ana's so far. Root has its own home, slash root, which is not the same as the root of the tree. Slash usr holds installed programs and their files. Slash bin is now only a link into slash usr slash bin, kept so old paths still work. Slash boot holds the kernel and bootloader. Slash dev holds devices, such as disks and terminals, as files. And slash proc is the strangest: it is not on any disk. The kernel invents it on the fly, and its numbered directories are the processes running right now, one per process ID. Learn this map once and every Linux server becomes readable, because they all follow it. When you wonder where something is, ask what kind of thing it is: configuration, changing data, a program, or a live view of the kernel. Next, moving around this tree.

At any moment, the shell has a current directory, and pwd, print working directory, shows it as a full path from the root. After login, Ana is in slash home slash ana. cd, change directory, moves her. cd slash etc uses an absolute path, one that starts with a slash, so it means the same thing from anywhere. Notice the prompt changes too: it now shows slash etc instead of the tilde. Inside slash etc, ls dash l lists three files by name. Those names are relative paths, read from the current directory. The table on the right reads one line column by column. The first character is the type: a dash for a regular file, d for a directory, and l for a symbolic link, a file that points at another file. Os-release is one such link, and the arrow shows where it points. The next nine characters are permissions, which the next course explains. Then the number of links, the owner and group, the size in bytes, the date of the last change, and the name. A link's size is the length of the path it points to, twenty one characters here. Two shortcuts finish the tour. Dot dot means the parent directory, so cd dot dot climbs one level, to slash. And cd on its own always takes you home. Next, reading what is inside these files.

Most of what a server admin reads is text, and Linux has a tool for each size of file. cat prints a whole file at once, which suits a short one like the hostname. For a long file, less shows one screen at a time. On the right is the SSH server's configuration file, open in less: the space bar pages down, a slash searches, and q quits. Lines starting with a hash are comments, the default values shown for reference. tail shows the end of a file; tail dash n five prints the last five lines. That matters for logs, which grow at the end, and the next courses use it constantly. Now the idea that makes Linux so easy to inspect: everything is a file. The special variable dollar dollar holds the shell's own process ID. Under slash proc, the kernel shows a directory for that process, full of files describing it, from its memory map to its open files. Two of them are on the right. Comm holds the process's name, bash: the shell Ana is typing into. And cwd is a link to its current working directory, slash home slash ana. No special tool was needed. The same cat and ls that read ordinary files can inspect a running program. That ends the first look around. Next, the people on this server, and what each of them may do.

Every Linux system has one all-powerful account, root, with user ID zero. The kernel lets root read any file and change anything, which is exactly why Ana never logs in as root. She logs in as herself and borrows root's power one command at a time, with sudo. The first command, id, shows what Ana is: user one thousand, and a member of a group called sudo. That group is her ticket. Asked to read the password file, slash etc slash shadow, as herself, she is refused. Put sudo in front of the same kind of command, and sudo asks for Ana's own password, not root's, then runs it as root, and the first line of the file appears. sudo whoami confirms it: for that one command, she was root. sudo dash l lists what Ana is allowed to do: all commands, as any user. And the last command shows the part that makes sudo better than a root login. Every command run through it is recorded in the system journal, with who ran it, where, and as whom. On the right, the Red Hat family does the same thing with a different group name, wheel, and greets each new user once with sudo's famous lecture. Next, who else lives on this server, and how Linux describes a user.

To Linux, a user is a line in a text file. getent passwd ana prints Ana's line from slash etc slash passwd, and the table on the right takes that format apart, using a new user, deploy. Ana's site will be copied onto the server by an automated deploy, and that job should not run as Ana, who can become root. So we add a separate user with no password at all, and no sudo. The line has seven fields separated by colons. The name, then an x, which says the real password hash is kept in the shadow file, which only root can read. Then the user ID and group ID. These numbers are what the kernel actually checks; the name is only a label for people. Then a free text comment, the home directory, and the login shell. id deploy shows its groups, and ls dash l on slash home shows two private home directories, each readable only by its owner. On Rocky Linux, the family card shows the same job done with useradd instead of Debian's friendlier adduser script. The real output differs in two small ways: Debian also put deploy in a group called users, and Rocky's ls shows a dot after the permissions, which marks a SELinux label. Next, what those permission letters actually mean.

Every file has an owner, a group, and three sets of permission bits: one for the owner, one for the group, and one for everyone else, called other. Each set says read, write and execute, shown as r, w and x, or a dash when the right is missing. When Ana touches a file, the kernel picks exactly one of those sets. Is she the owner? If not, is she in the file's group? If not, she is other, and only the last three bits count. The diagram on the right draws that check. Slash etc slash hostname belongs to root, and its other bits are r, dash, dash. So Ana can read it, and cat shows the hostname, but when she tries to write a new name into it, the shell is refused. The shadow file's other bits are three dashes, so even reading it is denied. The same letters mean slightly different things on a directory. Read lets you list the names inside, and execute lets you pass through it. Slash etc is r dash x for other, so Ana can list and enter it, while root's home directory is closed to everyone but root, so ls cannot even open it. Notice what never happened: Ana was never asked who she is. The kernel already knows, from her user ID, on every single access.

Ana's website needs a home, and it should belong to the deploy user. First, umask prints zero zero zero two. A umask is the set of bits a new file does not get: a file asks for read and write for everyone, the umask takes away write for other, and the result is the six six four the table on the right works through. Creating the web root under slash var slash www needs root, so Ana uses sudo, and the directory belongs to root. sudo chown hands it to deploy, as owner and group, and the second listing shows the change. Now deploy writes the first page, and its file comes out exactly as the umask predicted. Ana herself can no longer create files there: touch is refused, because for this directory she is other, with read and execute but no write. That is the point: only the deploy job can change the site. chmod changes permission bits, usually written as three octal digits, where read is four, write two, and execute one. Six four zero leaves other with nothing, and Ana's cat is refused. Six four four gives other read again, and the page prints. A web server reads the site as other too, so six four four is the mode every page will need. Next, a safer way for Ana herself to log in.

So far Ana has logged in with a password, which can be guessed, phished or reused. SSH keys replace it. On her laptop, the first listing shows she has no dot ssh directory yet. ssh-keygen makes a key pair, a matched private key and public key, using the modern Ed25519 algorithm. We left the passphrase empty to keep this short; on a real laptop, a passphrase protects the key if the laptop is stolen. The listing shows the difference between the two files. The private key is readable by Ana alone, and it never leaves the laptop. The public key is safe to give to anyone, and it is one line of text. ssh-copy-id logs in to web-01 one last time with the password, and appends that line to a file on the server called authorized keys. Then the real test: ssh to web-01 again, and this time no password is asked. The laptop offered the public key, the server found it in authorized keys, and the laptop then signed this session's data with the private key, a signature the server can check with the public key it holds. The private key itself never crossed the network. On the server, authorized keys holds exactly the public key, and SSH insists the file and its directory are private to Ana, or it ignores them. On a Mac, the card at the bottom shows the same OpenSSH built in, with ssh copy id included, so these steps work there unchanged. With a key that works, the passwords can now be switched off.

A server on the internet sees password guesses against its SSH port all day. Now that Ana's key works, two settings shut that door: no password logins, and no direct root logins. A change to SSH can lock you out, so it follows a careful order. First, sshd dash capital T prints the settings the SSH server will really use, after reading every configuration file. Right now passwords are allowed, and root may log in with a key. Ana writes the two new settings into their own small file in the sshd config dot d directory, rather than editing the main file. sshd dash t tests the configuration, and config OK means it parses. Only then does she reload the service. Reloading keeps every open session, including the one she is typing in. The effective settings now read no and no. Then the most important step: test from a second terminal, while the first is still logged in. Forcing a password login is now refused, with publickey as the only method offered. A normal login with her key still works. Only now is it safe to close the first session. If the test had failed, the first terminal could still undo the change. On Rocky Linux, the service is called sshd rather than ssh, and its drop-in directory already holds the distribution's own files. Ana's server now has its people and its locks.

Ana's server needs a web server program, and on Linux you do not download programs from websites. You install packages from your distribution's repositories. A package is an archive of files plus instructions: where each file goes, and which other packages it needs. On Debian, the list of repositories lives in debian dot sources, shown first. Each block names a source: the kind of packages, where to fetch them, which suites, and which components. Trixie is Debian thirteen itself, trixie updates carries its point releases, and backports offers newer versions only if you ask for them. Security fixes come from their own archive, trixie security. Main means free software only. The last field is the important one: signed by. It names the only keyring this source may be signed with, and the keyrings directory shows the keys Debian ships, one set per release. When Ana runs sudo apt update, apt downloads one small file per suite, called InRelease. It is the signed index: it carries the checksum of every package list, and apt verifies its signature against that keyring before trusting any of it. Then it fetches the lists themselves and stores them under slash var slash lib slash apt slash lists. Every package installed later is checked against those lists. A tampered mirror cannot slip in a file, because its checksum would not match a signed list. Next, the two commands everyone mixes up.

Two commands with similar names do very different jobs. sudo apt update refreshes what apt knows. It downloads the latest package lists from every source, so apt learns which versions exist today. It installs nothing; not a single program on the server changes. sudo apt upgrade changes what is installed. It compares each installed package with the lists, and replaces every one that has a newer version. That is why the order matters. Upgrade without updating first, and apt compares against old lists and quietly finds nothing to do. Between the two, apt list dash dash upgradable shows what an upgrade would replace, so you never upgrade blind. On this server, the honest answer is nothing. The update ends with all packages are up to date, the list of upgradable packages is empty, and the upgrade's summary reads upgrading zero. That is real: web-01 was built from an image that was current on the day these commands ran. A server that has run for a few weeks would list packages here, often including security fixes, and that is exactly why the next sections matter. The rule to remember is simple. Update first, to learn. Read the list. Then upgrade, to change. Next, we install the first package the website needs.

The web server Ana will use is nginx, one of the most popular on the internet. sudo apt install nginx asks for one package, but apt answers with two. Nginx itself depends on nginx common, so apt installs both. Notice that apt fetched them from the security archive: the newest version of nginx in trixie is a security update. While unpacking, one line stands out: created symlink, into a directory called multi user target wants. That is systemd being told to start nginx at every boot. The next course explains it. So where did everything go? dpkg dash L lists the files a package installed. The nginx package brings the program itself, in slash usr slash sbin, plus documentation. dpkg dash S answers the reverse question: which package owns this file? The main configuration file belongs to nginx common. The table on the right gathers the layout. The program under slash usr, configuration under slash etc slash nginx, the service unit that tells systemd how to run it, logs under slash var slash log slash nginx, and a default page under slash var slash www slash html. These are the same places the directory tour named. And on Debian, installing a service also starts it. systemctl says active, and curl, a command line web client, gets a two hundred OK straight back from the new server. Next, the same install on the Red Hat family.

Here is the same job on web-02, the Rocky Linux server, and it is worth seeing whole, because the families differ in more than the command's name. dnf install nginx resolves its dependencies and prints a table first: four packages, where Debian needed two. The program itself is nginx core, and rocky logos httpd provides the default page's images. rpm dash q f, the Red Hat family's way of asking which package owns a file, says the configuration belongs to nginx core. The configuration directory differs too. Debian splits sites into sites available and sites enabled; Rocky uses conf dot d, with no enabling step. The default page lives in slash usr slash share slash nginx slash html instead of slash var slash www. Then the biggest difference. systemctl is active says inactive. Red Hat's policy is that a newly installed service does not run until an administrator turns it on, so nothing listens on the network by surprise. One command does both halves: systemctl enable dash dash now, which sets it to start at boot and starts it now. Only then does curl get its two hundred OK, with a Server header that also reveals the version. Neither policy is wrong. Debian assumes you installed a service to use it; Red Hat makes you say so. Knowing which one you are on saves a confused hour. Next, keeping all of these packages up to date without being there.

Security fixes arrive all the time, and a server that waits for its admin to log in will miss some. Debian's cloud image already includes a tool for this, unattended upgrades, and the first command confirms it is installed. Is it switched on? Its settings live in a small file under apt dot conf dot d, and both lines say one: refresh the package lists every day, and run unattended upgrade every day. Who runs them? Two systemd timers, listed next: apt daily, which updates the lists, and apt daily upgrade, which installs. Their next run is shown, and nothing has run yet on this fresh server. Then a dry run asks what it would do right now, without changing anything. It names the allowed origins, Debian trixie and Debian security, so only fixes from Debian's own stable archives are installed automatically. It finds nothing to upgrade, for the same reason as before: the image is current. On Rocky Linux, the family card shows the opposite starting point. The equivalent tool, dnf automatic, is not installed at all. Ana installs it and enables its timer, but its configuration reveals a catch: apply updates equals no. Out of the box it only downloads updates and applies nothing, until that line is changed. Whichever family you run, check rather than assume. Ana's server can now install and patch software. Next, the programs that run all the time.

Every running program on Linux is a process, and every process has a number, its process ID, and a parent, the process that started it. ps prints both. The first row is process one, slash sbin slash init, whose parent is zero: the kernel itself started it. The second is Ana's own shell. pstree draws the whole family as a tree, and the picture on the right redraws it. At the root is systemd, the program behind process one. Everything else descends from it. The SSH server, sshd, started a session for Ana's login, and that session started her bash shell, which is running pstree right now. Nginx appears with two children: a master process and its workers. The ps listing of nginx shows why there are two kinds. The master runs as root, because only root may open port eighty and read every configuration file. Its workers run as www dash data, an unprivileged user, and they are the ones that answer requests. If a worker were ever tricked into misbehaving, it would hold none of root's power. You will also spot qemu ga: the virtual machine provider's agent, which this course's servers have because they are virtual machines. Finally, slash proc slash one slash exe is a link to the program process one is running. Ana needs sudo even to read it, and it points to systemd. Next, how you tell a process to stop.

Processes are controlled with signals: short messages the kernel delivers to a process. kill dash l lists them by number and name. Despite its name, the kill command only sends a signal, and by default it sends TERM, number fifteen, which means: please stop. A process may catch TERM and run its own cleanup first. To see that, we start a small background program that sets a trap: when it receives TERM, it prints a message and exits. Then kill sends TERM to it. The trap runs, the message appears, and the job ends normally, reported as done. Now the same program, but trapping KILL instead. kill dash KILL sends signal nine. This time nothing is printed. KILL can never be caught, blocked or ignored: the kernel simply removes the process, mid step, and the shell reports it as killed. Any cleanup it would have done, closing files, finishing a write, removing a lock, never happens. That is the whole difference, and it gives us a rule. Always ask first with TERM, give the process a moment, and only then force it with KILL. systemd follows the same rule when it stops a service: it sends a polite signal, waits for a timeout, and only then kills what is left. The table on the right adds two more you will meet: INT, which Control C sends, and HUP, which many daemons treat as reload your configuration. Next, the program that manages all the services: systemd.

systemd starts, stops and watches every service on the server, and systemctl is how you talk to it. systemctl status nginx is the first command to run when anything seems wrong, and the table on the right reads it. Loaded names the unit file systemd read, and says enabled, which means nginx will start at boot. Active says it is running, and since when. Main PID is the nginx master. And the CGroup lists every process belonging to the service, the master and both workers. systemd tracks them as a group, so when it stops nginx, no stray child is left behind. systemctl cat shows the unit file itself. A unit is a small text file in sections. Service says how to run the program: test the configuration first, then start it, and how to reload and stop it. Install has one line, wanted by multi user target, which the next section uses. The unit section holds the dependencies, and this is where many people get confused. Wants and Requires answer one question: should starting nginx also start something else? Requires is the strict version: if that unit fails, nginx is stopped too. After answers a different question: if both are starting, which goes first? After alone never starts anything. systemctl show prints the full, real lists, including the ones systemd adds by itself. Nginx wants the network to be online, and is ordered after it. Next, the difference between enabling a service and starting it.

Two separate switches control every service. Enabled or disabled decides what happens at the next boot. Active or inactive is what is happening right now. Many outages come from mixing them up, so this section proves the difference with a real reboot, run from Ana's laptop because a reboot ends any session on the server. At first, nginx is enabled and active. Ana disables it. systemd removes a symbolic link from the multi user target's wants directory, the boot list. Then both switches are read again: disabled, but still active. Nginx is still running and still serving the site. Disabling stopped nothing. It only changed the next boot. Then sudo reboot. The connection closes, the server restarts, and Ana logs in again. Uptime confirms the machine has only just come back. Now nginx is disabled and inactive: nothing started it, and the website is down. This is the trap. A change made with disable, or a service started by hand and never enabled, looks fine until the next reboot, perhaps weeks later, at three in the morning. The fix is one command with both halves: enable dash dash now. It creates the link for the next boot, and starts the service immediately. Both switches read enabled and active again. After any change to a service, check both switches. Next, where services write what they are doing.

When a service misbehaves, the first question is: what did it say? On a systemd server, the kernel, systemd itself, and every service send their messages to one place, the journal, kept by systemd journald. journalctl reads it. Ana's first attempt shows no entries, with a hint: the system's log is only for root and for members of the adm and systemd journal groups. With sudo, journalctl dash u nginx shows the entries for one unit: systemd starting nginx, and started. Dash b limits the view to the current boot, and its first lines are the kernel's own, from the very start of that boot. The same filter works on any unit. For ssh, dash n four shows the last four entries: the SSH server listening on port twenty two, and a session being opened for Ana's own login. Then Ana reloads nginx and reads its journal again. Three lines tell the story: systemd reloading, nginx starting a signal process, and systemd reporting reloaded. The table on the right has one more filter, dash f, which follows the journal live, printing new entries as they arrive, until Control C. Logs, filtered by unit, by boot, by count: that habit will save hours. Next, what happens before any of this, at boot.

Between pressing the power button and a login prompt, a Linux server hands control along a short chain, and every link in it left a trace that web-01 can show us. The top row is that chain. First comes the firmware, built into the machine; here it is the virtual machine's own. It finds the memory, which the kernel later reports as the BIOS RAM map, and starts a bootloader from the disk. On Debian the bootloader is GRUB, which lives in slash boot slash grub. GRUB loads two files from slash boot, listed in the table: vmlinuz, the compressed kernel, and initrd, the initial RAM disk. It also passes the kernel a command line, which slash proc slash cmdline still shows: which kernel image, which partition holds the root filesystem, and to mount it read only at first. The kernel starts, and the journal's first line is its own announcement, Linux version six point twelve. It unpacks the initial RAM disk and runs slash init from it: a tiny system whose one job is to find and mount the real root disk. Then it hands over to systemd, which becomes process number one, the ancestor of every other process. systemd starts the services, in dependency order, until it reaches the multi-user target: networking and SSH are up, and logins are open. This virtual machine is emulated, so its timings are slow and say nothing about real hardware. What matters is the order, and that every step of it is written down.

Nginx is installed and running, but it is serving Debian's default page. Ana's site needs its own configuration. The main file, nginx dot conf, mostly includes other files, and the last include is the one that matters: everything in sites enabled. Debian keeps two directories. Sites available is a shelf of configurations, and sites enabled holds links to the ones nginx should actually read. Right now one link is enabled, default, and its server block, with comments stripped, listens on port eighty for any name and serves slash var slash www slash html. Ana writes a server block of her own, shown on the right. It is six lines. Listen on port eighty. Server name says which website this block answers for: requests for ana dot example. Root is the directory the files come from, the web root that the deploy user owns. And index names the file to serve when someone asks for a directory. Then she enables it the Debian way, with a symbolic link from sites enabled to the file in sites available, and removes the link to the default site. The file itself stays on the shelf, so disabling a site later is just deleting a link. On Rocky Linux, the family card shows a simpler layout. There are no sites directories at all; nginx reads every file ending in dot conf in conf dot d, so a file there is enabled by existing. Nginx has not read any of this yet. Next, we put the site's files in place.

Ana writes her website on her laptop, in a folder called site, and the server only ever receives copies. The tool for that is rsync. It copies files over SSH, and it is clever about it: it compares both sides and sends only what is missing or has changed. Ana runs it as the deploy user, which owns the web root and has no sudo. Deploy logs in with a key that was installed for it beforehand, so no password is involved. Two details of the command matter. Dash a, archive, copies whole directory trees and keeps permissions and times. And the trailing slash after site means: copy the contents of this folder, not the folder itself. Without it, the files would land in a subfolder called site. The first run sends everything: the directory, about dot html and index dot html. ssh as deploy lists the web root, and the files are there, owned by deploy. Then, from the laptop, curl asks for ana dot example, and the page comes back. Nginx served it straight away; there was nothing to restart. Ana adds a line to her index page and runs exactly the same command again. This time rsync sends only index dot html, the one file that changed. That is what makes it a deploy tool: the same command, every time, and it does the least work needed. The new line appears on the live site. One note for Mac users: the rsync Apple ships is openrsync, which reports an older protocol version, but the options used here mean the same thing. Next, the safe way to change nginx's configuration.

Every change to nginx's configuration follows the same two steps: test, then reload. sudo nginx dash t reads every configuration file and checks it without touching the running server: syntax is ok, test is successful. Before reloading, ps lists the nginx processes: one master and two workers. Then sudo systemctl reload nginx, and ps again. Compare the two listings in the table on the right. The master has the same process ID: it was never stopped. The workers have new IDs. On a reload, the master re-reads the configuration and starts fresh workers with it, while the old workers finish the requests they were serving and then exit. No visitor is cut off. A restart is different: it stops the master and everything with it, and open connections are dropped. Now the reason to test first. Ana deliberately writes a broken file, a server block with a missing semicolon. nginx dash t catches it immediately, names the file and the line, and says test failed. What if someone reloads anyway? systemd reports that the job failed, but systemctl is active still says active. The reload was refused, and nginx kept serving with its old, working configuration. Had this been a restart, nginx would have stopped and the site would be down. Ana removes the broken file and the test passes again. Test, then reload: a habit that turns a typo into an error message instead of an outage. Next, how the server is connected to the network.

Before the site can be reached, three questions have answers on the server itself. First: what is my address? ip addr lists the network interfaces. Lo, the loopback, is the machine talking to itself at one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one. Ens three is the real network card, with the address one nine two dot zero dot two dot ten, slash twenty four. The slash twenty four says how big the local network is: every address that starts with one nine two dot zero dot two. Second: where do packets go? ip route answers. Addresses on that local network are reached directly, straight out of ens three. Everything else follows the default route, to the gateway, a router that forwards it toward the rest of the internet. Third: how does a name become an address? The resolver file points at one two seven dot zero dot zero dot fifty three, a small local resolver run by systemd resolved. But the order of the search is set in nsswitch dot conf: files first, which means slash etc slash hosts, then the local resolver, then DNS. getent asks exactly the way programs do. deb dot debian dot org comes back from DNS with four addresses. Ana dot example comes back with web-01's own address, and grep shows why: a line in slash etc slash hosts. That is a stand in, and it says so in its own comment. Ana dot example is a name reserved for documentation, so it can never be in public DNS. On a Mac, as the card shows, ip and ss do not exist at all: macOS has the older ifconfig and netstat instead. Next, a request's whole journey.

What actually happens when someone opens http colon slash slash ana dot example? curl dash v shows every step, and the top row of the picture follows them. Lines starting with a star are curl talking about itself, greater than signs are what it sent, and less than signs are what came back. First, the name. Ana dot example resolves to one nine two dot zero dot two dot ten, here through the hosts file standing in for DNS. Second, a connection: curl opens a TCP connection to port eighty, and the server's kernel accepts it on behalf of nginx. With HTTPS, an encrypted TLS handshake would happen at this point; that comes two sections from now. Third, the request itself, a few lines of plain text. GET slash asks for the root of the site. And the Host header names the website, because one server can host many sites on one address. Fourth, nginx. It matches the Host header against each server block's server name, picks Ana's block, takes its root, adds the index file, and finds index dot html on disk. Fifth, the answer. A status line, two hundred OK, then headers: who answered, the type of content, its length, and when the file last changed. A blank line, then the page itself. The second command asks for a file that does not exist, and the status line says four oh four, not found. The table on the right lists the codes this course will meet. Next, the doors that let requests in: ports.

A server program does not simply listen to the network. It asks the kernel for a port, and the kernel hands it a socket, a kind of file that connections arrive through. ss shows every listening socket. With dash t for TCP, l for listening, and n for numbers instead of names, the list is short. Ports eighty and twenty two are open on zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, which means every IPv4 address the machine has. Port fifty three is open only on one two seven addresses, so only programs on this machine can use it: that is the local name resolver. Adding dash p shows which process owns each socket, and that needs sudo. Port eighty belongs to nginx: three process IDs, the master and both workers, sharing one socket. The master opened it as root, then handed it to workers that run without root. Port twenty two belongs to sshd. One line deserves a second look. Port fifty three fifty five is open on every address, IPv4 and IPv6, for systemd resolved. It is LLMNR, a protocol for finding machines by name on a local network, which a web server does not need. It is not a hole by itself, but every open port is something that can be reached, and a later review on this server will ask why each one is open. The rule to keep: if a port is listening on an address the world can reach, you should know why. Next, encrypting the website with HTTPS.

Right now the site only speaks plain HTTP, and from the server itself, a request to HTTPS fails: nothing listens on port four four three. HTTPS needs a certificate: a document that binds the name ana dot example to a key, signed by a certificate authority that browsers already trust. Let's Encrypt gives these away for free, through a protocol called ACME, and certbot is the client. One honest note first. Ana dot example is a documentation name that can never be in public DNS, so Let's Encrypt cannot reach it. Instead, this course runs Pebble, a small local ACME certificate authority, playing Let's Encrypt's part. Certbot and every step are real; only the server address on the command line differs. After installing certbot and its nginx plugin, one command does the job. Certbot proves to the authority that it controls ana dot example, receives a certificate valid for ninety days, and saves it with its key under slash etc slash letsencrypt slash live. With the nginx plugin, it also edits Ana's server block: it adds listen four four three ssl and the two certificate files, and turns the old port eighty block into a redirect. It sets up automatic renewal, so the ninety days never run out. From the laptop, HTTPS now answers two hundred OK, and plain HTTP answers three oh one, moved permanently, pointing visitors to the secure address. The last command prints the chain the server sends: Ana's certificate, signed by an intermediate, signed by a root that the laptop trusts. Next, closing every door except these.

Every listening socket is reachable from the internet unless something stands in front of it. Before starting, the laptop reaches a test service on port eighty eighty: something set up beforehand, to stand for a program that should not be public. Debian's cloud image has no firewall rules at all; it does not even have the nft tool. Ana installs nftables, the Linux kernel's firewall framework, and writes its configuration file. The important line is policy drop: anything not explicitly accepted is silently dropped. Then the accept rules, read from top to bottom. Traffic on the loopback. Replies to connections the server started itself, called established and related, so that apt can still download updates. Ports twenty two, eighty and four four three, for SSH and the website. And pings. nft dash c checks the file without applying it: syntax OK. Then enable dash dash now applies it, and makes it permanent across reboots. Because a firewall mistake can lock Ana out, the test happens from a second terminal while the first stays logged in. SSH still works: hostname answers web-01. The website still answers two hundred. And port eighty eighty, which answered before, now returns three zeros after a five second timeout. The firewall dropped the packets without a reply, so curl gave up. Only now is it safe to close the first session. On Rocky Linux, the family card shows the same starting point: no firewall running. The Red Hat family's usual tool is firewalld, and Ubuntu's is ufw, both front ends to the same kernel firewall. Next, a second lock that Red Hat adds.

This section happens on web-02, the Rocky Linux server, because it shows a lock that permissions alone cannot explain. Ana builds her site in her home directory, then moves it into slash var slash www with sudo mv. ls dash l shows what looks perfect: the file is readable by everyone. Yet nginx answers four oh three, forbidden. Notice the dot after the permissions. It means the file also carries a SELinux label. SELinux is mandatory access control: on top of the usual permission check, the kernel checks a policy about which kinds of processes may touch which kinds of files, and both checks must pass. The audit log records the refusal, and the picture reads it field by field. Denied: read. The process: nginx, running in the domain h t t p d underscore t. The file's label: user home t, which means a file from someone's home directory. The policy does not let a web server read home directory files, and the label came along with the move. mv keeps a file's label; a newly created file would have taken its directory's label instead. ls dash capital Z confirms it. The fix has two parts. semanage fcontext adds a permanent rule saying that everything under this web root is web content. restorecon then applies the rule to the files that exist, relabeling them httpd sys content t. And nginx answers two hundred OK. The temptation is to switch SELinux off. Don't. Read the denial, then fix the label. Debian has its own mandatory access control, AppArmor. Correct permissions are not the same as access. The site is online, encrypted and guarded. Next, the logs it produces.

Every process starts with three open streams, numbered zero, one and two. Standard input, zero, is where it reads. Standard output, one, is for its results. Standard error, two, is for its complaints. In a terminal, both outputs are shown on screen, so they look the same, but they are separate, and the first command shows it. Ana asks ls for two paths, one real and one missing. The result line goes to standard output, and the error goes to standard error. A greater than sign redirects standard output into a file. Run it again with that, and the error still appears on screen: only stream one went to the file, and cat confirms the file holds just the result. To capture both, add two greater than ampersand one, which means: send stream two wherever stream one is going. Now the screen is silent and the file has both lines. Here is the classic trap. Write the same two redirections in the opposite order, and the error appears on screen again. Redirections are applied left to right. Two to one first copies where stream one points at that moment, which is still the terminal. Only afterwards does stream one move to the file. The diagram draws both orders. The last command adds a pipe, which connects one program's standard output to the next program's standard input. ls is asked for two directories, one of them missing; its error is thrown away into slash dev slash null, and wc dash l counts the lines that survive. Next, these tools put to work on the web server's log.

Nginx writes one line to its access log for every request it answers. On this server the log holds twenty four lines. One honest note: these visits were replayed beforehand with curl, each claiming to be a particular browser, a search engine crawler, or a scanner. Nginx and its log are real; the visitors are stand ins. tail shows two lines, and the table on the right splits one on its spaces: the client's address, the time, the request's path in field seven, the status code in field nine, and the bytes sent. grep dash c counts matching lines: six requests got a four oh four. Now, which pages are popular? cut dash d space dash f seven keeps only the path, and uniq dash c counts repeated lines. But look at the result. The front page appears three times, counted nine, then one, then three. That is not a bug in uniq. It only merges lines that are next to each other, and the paths arrive in the order the visits happened. The fix is to sort first, so equal paths sit side by side. Then uniq dash c counts each group once, and a second sort, numeric and reversed, puts the biggest count on top: thirteen visits to the front page, five to about. Further down are paths that this site never had: wp login, dot env, dot git slash config. Those are automated probes, looking for a forgotten admin page or a leaked secret. Every public server sees them. Next, a tool that understands fields properly: awk.

cut is good for one field. For anything more, there is awk, a small language built for exactly this kind of text. An awk program is a list of patterns, each with an action in braces, and awk runs it on every line of its input. Dollar nine means the ninth field. So awk print dollar nine prints every status code, and sorted and counted, the answer is eighteen successes and six not founds. Add a pattern in front: dollar nine equals four oh four. Now the action runs only for the lines that match, printing the path that failed. All five are probes for files this site never had. The user agent, the text that names the browser, contains spaces, so splitting on spaces would cut it into pieces. Dash capital F changes the separator to the double quote, and then the user agent is field six. Counted, the visitors are Firefox, Safari, Google's crawler, and zgrab, a scanner that sweeps the internet looking for weaknesses. The last program shows awk's memory. It adds field ten, the bytes sent, into a variable as it reads each line. The END block runs once, after the last line, and prints the total, together with NR, the number of records read: twenty four requests. Remember that these visits were replayed for the course, but every number here was computed from the real log. Next, Ana stops typing commands by hand and writes a script.

Ana deploys her site with the same rsync command every time, so she puts it in a script, shown on the right. The first line, the shebang, says which program runs the file: bash. Then two variables. In bash there are no spaces around the equals sign, and a dollar sign reads the value back. Notice the quotes around dollar site dir: if a path ever contains a space, the quotes keep it one word instead of two. chmod plus x makes the file executable, and the script runs, says done, and dollar question mark, the exit code of the last command, is zero, which means success. Now the important test: what happens when something goes wrong? Ana renames her site folder, so there is nothing to deploy, and runs the script again. rsync fails, loudly, with error code twenty three. And then the script prints done anyway. Worse, its exit code is zero, success. A script's exit code is simply the exit code of its last command, and the last command was echo, which worked. To anything that calls this script, a timer, another script, a monitoring check, this broken deploy looks perfect. Bash, by default, keeps going after a command fails. That made sense for typing at a prompt; it is dangerous in a script. Ana puts her folder back. Next, making the script stop when something fails.

The new version of deploy dot sh, on the right, adds three things at the top. set dash e makes the script stop at the first command that fails. Dash u turns an unset variable into an error, so a typo in a variable's name stops the script instead of silently becoming an empty string. And dash o pipefail makes a pipeline fail if any part of it fails, not just the last. Together they are the standard first line of a careful bash script. The trap line prints which line failed, on standard error, whenever a command fails. These have limits, listed in the table. set dash e does not trigger for a command inside an if condition, or on the left of and and or, because there the failure is being tested on purpose. So a script also checks, explicitly, for what it needs. Before touching the server, an if asks whether the site's index file exists. If not, it prints why, on standard error, and exits with one. Ana runs the same test as before, with the site folder moved away. This time the script refuses straight away with a clear message, and the exit code is one: failure, which anything calling the script can see. Notice the trap stayed quiet: an explicit exit one is a decision, not an error. With the folder back, the deploy runs and exits zero. A script that tells the truth about failing is the only kind worth automating. Next, running a job on a schedule.

Ana wants a small report every night: how many requests got each status code. On a systemd server, a scheduled job is two units. The service says what to run. It is type oneshot, a command that runs and exits, here the awk report from earlier. The timer says when. On calendar, every day at two in the morning. Persistent true means that if the server was off at two, the job runs as soon as it boots, instead of being skipped. And the install section makes the timer part of timers target, so it starts at boot. Both files are shown on the right as they were written. After daemon reload, which tells systemd to read new unit files, Ana enables and starts the timer, not the service. list timers shows the next run, tonight at two. There is no need to wait until then: starting the service by hand runs the job right now, and its output goes to the journal under its own unit. journalctl shows the report, eighteen two hundreds and six four oh fours, between systemd's starting and finished lines. The traditional tool for this is cron, and the table compares them. With a timer, the output is in the journal, a missed run can catch up, and you can test the job any time. This image does ship a few cron files, but cron itself is not even running: on a modern Debian server, timers already do this work. Next, keeping those logs from growing forever.

Every request adds a line to the access log, and nothing ever removes one. Left alone, logs grow until the disk is full. The standard answer is logrotate, and nginx ships its own rotation rules, the first file shown. Read on the right: rotate daily, keep fourteen old logs, compress them, but delay compression by one rotation so yesterday's log stays readable, create the new log with the right owner and mode, and after rotating, tell nginx to reopen its files, because a running program keeps writing to the file it already has open. The logs are small for now. Ana forces a rotation to see it happen, and the system answers: command not found. This is a real finding. Debian thirteen's cloud image does not include logrotate, even though nginx installed a configuration for it. On this server, the logs would never have rotated, and nothing would have complained until the disk filled. That is exactly the kind of thing a review finds, and why the last course has one. Installing logrotate also enables its timer, which list timers shows will run tonight. Ana forces a rotation now. The listing shows the result: access log and error log are new, empty files, and yesterday's content has moved to dot one. Tomorrow, dot one becomes dot two and is compressed, and after fourteen days the oldest is deleted. The server now looks after its own logs. Next, the final course: keeping the server running.

Servers run out of disk, and the first time it happens it is usually a log. For this section, a three gigabyte access log was created beforehand, standing in for a log that grew for months. Everything after that is real. df dash h asks the filesystem how full it is: forty two percent. du dash s h adds up the sizes of files it can find, and slash var slash log slash nginx holds three point one gigabytes, almost all of it in access dot log. The obvious move is to delete it, so Ana does. du now says eight kilobytes. But df still says forty two percent. Not one byte was freed. Here is why. rm does not delete data; it removes a name. The file's data is freed only when nothing refers to it any more, and nginx's workers still have the file open, writing to it. find searches every process's open files under slash proc for ones marked deleted, and there they are: three nginx processes, each holding the deleted log on file descriptor twelve. du cannot see the file, because it has no name. df still counts its blocks, because they are still in use. The space comes back the moment nginx lets go: a reload makes nginx reopen its log files, and df drops to twenty percent. The lesson is to never delete a log that a program has open. Rotate it, which tells the program to reopen, or empty it in place with truncate. Next, the two numbers people misread most: memory and load.

free dash h is often read as: how much memory is left. The column called free is the wrong one to read. Free is memory that has never been used at all. Linux deliberately uses spare memory as a cache of file data, shown as buff slash cache, because reading a file from memory is far faster than from disk. When a program needs memory, the kernel simply drops some cache. So the number to read is available: free plus the cache that can be given back. Slash proc slash meminfo, where free gets its numbers, says the same in kilobytes. The other misread number is load. nproc says this server has two CPUs, and uptime shows three load averages, over one, five and fifteen minutes. Load is not a percentage. It is the average number of tasks that are running or waiting to run. To see it, Ana starts four copies of yes, a program that does nothing but use CPU, on a server with two CPUs. A minute later, the one minute load has climbed past three, and it is still rising toward four, while the five and fifteen minute averages lag behind. top shows why: zero percent idle, both CPUs busy all the time, and four processes sharing them, so at any moment two are waiting. A load equal to the number of CPUs means fully busy. Higher means a queue. After killing the yes processes, uptime still shows the high load: averages take time to fall. Next, the job that matters most when something goes badly wrong: backups.

Everything on web-01 could be lost tomorrow: a failed disk, a mistaken command, a provider closing an account. A backup is a copy somewhere else. Ana keeps hers on her laptop, a different machine, so that one failure cannot take both. rsync dash a pulls the web root from the server into a backups folder, and the listing shows both files. Is that a backup? Not yet. A backup you have never restored is a hope. So Ana tests a restore, the part most people skip. She restores the backup into a scratch directory in slash tmp, never on top of anything real, and diff dash r compares the two trees file by file: the restore matches the backup. Then the stronger check, against the server itself. sha256sum computes a fingerprint of each file's exact bytes, on the server over SSH, and on the restored copy. The picture lines them up: about dot html and index dot html have identical fingerprints on both sides. The restore is byte for byte what is live. Three rules come out of this. Keep backups on another machine. Do not confuse redundancy with backup: a mirrored disk copies your mistakes instantly. And it only counts as a backup once a restore has been tested. A real server would also back up its configuration, under slash etc, and its certificates; the method is the same. Next, what to do when the site goes down.

Sooner or later, someone says: the site is down. The worst response is to guess. The best is to climb a ladder, one rung at a time, each rung ruling something out. For this section, two faults were made beforehand, on purpose, the kind a hurried edit makes; finding them is real. First rung, the name: from the laptop, getent resolves ana dot example to the right address. Ana logs in. Second rung, the port: curl cannot connect at all, which means nothing is listening on port eighty, so the problem is not the network, but the program. Third rung, the service: systemctl says nginx failed. Its journal says the configuration test failed, and nginx dash t names the exact place: an unexpected closing brace, line six of Ana's site file. The index line is missing its semicolon. sed adds it, the test passes, and nginx starts. Is the site back? curl now connects, but the answer is four oh three, forbidden. Fourth rung, permissions. ls dash l shows index dot html is readable only by its owner, deploy. Nginx's workers run as www data, who counts as other, and other has no read bit. chmod six four four, and the answer is two hundred OK, from the server and from the laptop. Two faults, and one would have hidden the other. Without the ladder, someone might have restarted things at random, or blamed the network. Next, checking the whole server before anything goes wrong.

A review asks a few plain questions of a server, regularly, before an attacker does. The table on the right lists them, with web-01's real answers. What is listening? ss shows SSH on twenty two and nginx on eighty, plus port fifty three fifty five, the name protocol flagged when we first met sockets. It is not needed. It is also harmless here, because the next answer covers it. Who can log in over SSH? sshd dash capital T confirms the lockdown from course two: no root login, no passwords, keys only. Who can become root? The sudo group holds only ana. Which accounts have a login shell? root, which has no password and may not log in over SSH; ana; deploy, by design, so rsync can reach it; and sync, a standard Debian account. What gets through the firewall? The policy is drop, with only twenty two, eighty and four four three accepted, so port fifty three fifty five listens, but no one outside can reach it. And what is out of date? apt list upgradable is empty, and the services that matter, including unattended upgrades and the firewall, are all active. This is defence in layers. The firewall covers for a service listening by accident. Keys cover for weak passwords. Automatic updates cover for the time between reviews. No layer is perfect; together they forgive each other's mistakes. Next, the one update that needs a reboot.

Almost any package can be updated while the server runs; the program is replaced and restarted. The kernel is different, because it is the thing everything else runs on. A new kernel is installed beside the running one, and only a reboot switches to it. So there are three questions, and three different places to look. Which kernel is running? uname dash r: six point twelve point one one three. Which kernels are installed? dpkg lists the kernel packages, and slash boot holds one kernel file. Is a reboot needed? On Debian, when an update requires one, a file appears: slash run slash reboot required. Here it does not exist. The honest answer today is that there is nothing to do. web-01's kernel is already the newest one Debian's security archive offers. apt cache policy shows where each version comes from. The installed version came from trixie security. An older one is the version Debian thirteen was released with. And a much newer kernel, seven point two, sits in backports, with a priority of one hundred, which means apt never chooses it on its own; you would have to ask for it explicitly. When a kernel security update does arrive, the sequence is the diagram on the right. The upgrade installs the new kernel, the reboot required file appears, uname still shows the old kernel, and only after a reboot does GRUB start the new one. Check uname afterwards: until it changes, the fix is not running. Next, a runbook, and where to go from here.

This is the server Ana built, on one map. Visitors reach it over HTTPS and Ana over SSH, both through a firewall that drops everything else. Inside, systemd runs every service: SSH with keys only, nginx serving ana dot example, the journal collecting what they say, and timers for security updates, the nightly report and log rotation. Under systemd is the Linux kernel, and under that, a small virtual machine. Two people have accounts, Ana as the admin, and deploy, who owns the website's files and nothing else. Her laptop holds the key, the deploy script, and a tested backup. Every part on the map names the section that built it. On the right is a runbook: for each symptom, the first command to reach for, every one of them met in this course. Site down: status, then the configuration test. A four oh three: the permissions, and on Red Hat, the SELinux label. A full disk: df, then du. Slow: uptime, free and top, read correctly. Anything strange: the journal. And before every change: test it, reload, and keep a second session open. Below it is what this course left out on purpose, because web-01 never needed it: disk partitioning and LVM, cgroups and namespaces, which are how containers are built, the firewall's internals, how a shell starts programs, regular expressions in depth, and the vim editor. Each is a good next step. The habits are the real lesson: observe before changing, test before reloading, and prove a backup by restoring it.
